theory.title: Half and full adders
theory.body: A half adder is Sum = A XOR B and Carry = A AND B. A full adder also takes Cin: Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin, Cout is 1 when at least two of A, B, Cin are 1. Two half adders plus an OR make a full adder.

guide: Toggle A and B on the half adder.
Turn Cin on and read the full-adder sum and Cout.
Switch the full-adder view between gates and half-adders.
Check all eight full-adder rows by toggling.
takeaways: Sum is XOR. Carry is AND for a half adder.
Cout is the majority of A, B, and Cin.
Carry and signed overflow are different flags on a wider adder.

theory.title: Ripple and look-ahead
theory.body: A ripple adder chains Cout of bit i into Cin of bit i+1, so delay grows with width. Carry look-ahead computes group generate/propagate so carries do not wait for every XOR. Carry-select duplicates slices and muxes on the incoming carry.

guide: Widen the word and watch the carry walk on ripple.
Switch to look-ahead and compare when Cout appears.
Try carry-select on the same operands.
Read unsigned sum versus the binary layout.
takeaways: Ripple delay grows with width.
Look-ahead does not wait for every stage.
The numeric sum is the same; the carry path is the lesson.

theory.title: Subtract by adding
theory.body: A − B is A + two's complement of B. Invert B and add 1 via Cin = 1 on an adder. A half/full subtractor uses Difference = A XOR B XOR Bin and a borrow-out when A is smaller than B plus Bin.

guide: Switch ADD to SUB and see B invert.
Compare increment and decrement.
Read borrow versus carry on the subtractor.
Watch flags after a wrap.
takeaways: Subtract is add of inverted B plus 1.
Borrow means the unsigned difference needed a wrap.
Increment is add 1; decrement is subtract 1.

theory.title: Magnitude compare
theory.body: A comparator reports A>B, A=B, or A<B. Unsigned compare walks from the MSB. Signed compare uses two's complement: the sign bits participate, so 1000 is less than 0111 in 4-bit two's complement (−8 < 7).

guide: Set two words and read >, =, <.
Flip the MSB and see unsigned versus signed disagree.
Equal words light only A=B.
Use the same ALU flags mentally: Z for equal, N and V for signed less.
takeaways: Unsigned and signed compare are different readings of the same bits.
Equality is bitwise match.
MSB-first is how a magnitude comparator is built.

theory.title: Shifters
theory.body: Logical left shift inserts 0s on the right. Logical right inserts 0s on the left. Arithmetic right copies the sign bit. A rotate wraps bits around the ends. Shift amount is a count, not a second data word's full value unless masked.

guide: Pick a shift kind and an amount.
Watch bits walk and what fills the hole.
Try arithmetic right on a negative two's-complement word.
Rotate and confirm nothing is lost.
takeaways: Logical right fills 0; arithmetic right fills the sign.
Left shift by k multiplies unsigned values by 2^k if it fits.
Rotate preserves all bits.

theory.title: ALU operations and flags
theory.body: An ALU muxes add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, and shifts onto one result bus. Flags: Z (result is 0), N (MSB is 1), C (unsigned carry/borrow), V (two's-complement overflow). The opcode selects the operation; the flags describe the result.

guide: Choose an ALU op and two operands.
Read Z, N, C, V after each result.
Force overflow with two large signed addends.
AND/OR/XOR leave C and V as this lab defines for logic.
takeaways: One datapath, many ops, selected by opcode.
C is unsigned carry; V is signed overflow.
Z is 1 only when every result bit is 0.

theory.title: Shift-add multiply and divide
theory.body: Binary multiply adds a shifted copy of the multiplicand for each 1 in the multiplier. Divide restores or subtracts and shifts the remainder. Partial products in this lab are teaching steps, not a Wallace tree.

guide: Step a multiply and read each partial product.
Try divide and watch the remainder.
Widen if the product does not fit.
Compare the final product with A × B in decimal.
takeaways: Multiply is add-and-shift.
A 0 in the multiplier skips that partial product.
Divide is subtract-and-shift with a remainder.

theory.title: Boolean expressions
theory.body: AND, OR, and NOT combine 0/1 variables. The parser builds a tree; evaluation walks that tree. Two expressions are equal when they produce the same output on every assignment.

guide: Build the expression with the keypad, or type it.
Read the Venn diagram, K-map, cube, and gate tree together.
Toggle A, B, and C. Every figure highlights the same live row.
Check a second expression in the equivalence panel.
takeaways: The engine parses a tree; it does not call eval().
Each Venn region and K-map cell is one minterm.
The gate tree, table, and diagram all evaluate that same tree.
play.what: The keypad and the text field write the same expression.
play.why: Every figure is a view of one truth table.
play.notice: Venn diagrams are drawn for one, two, and three variables. Four variables use the K-map.

theory.title: Boolean identities
theory.body: De Morgan, absorption, idempotent, and the other listed laws are equalities: both sides match on every input. You can try to break a law by toggling; if both sides stay equal, the identity holds in this algebra.

guide: Pick a law and read both sides.
Toggle the variables used in that law.
Confirm the two sides stay equal.
Open De Morgan next to absorption and see they are different rewrites.
takeaways: A law is an identity, not a suggestion.
De Morgan: (AB)' = A' + B' and (A+B)' = A'B'.
Absorption: A + AB = A.
laws.what: Each law is checked by evaluating both sides on the live assignment.
laws.why: If a rewrite were wrong, some toggle would make the sides differ.
laws.notice: These are two-level Boolean identities, not timing or voltage rules.

theory.title: Algebraic simplification
theory.body: Simplification applies identities to drop redundant terms. The lab shows a sequence of rewrites toward fewer operators. Quine–McCluskey on the truth table is the same function with a different algorithm.

guide: Enter an expression such as A + AB.
Read each rewrite step.
Compare the simplified form with the original table.
Try a larger SOP and see which terms survive.
takeaways: A + AB = A is absorption.
The simplified expression must match the original truth table.
Fewer operators is a cost metric, not a unique normal form.
simplify.what: Each step names the identity it used.
simplify.why: You should be able to justify every dropped literal.
simplify.notice: This simplifier is teaching-scale; huge expressions belong on the K-map or QM tabs.

theory.title: SOP and POS
theory.body: Sum of products is OR of AND terms (minterms or larger products). Product of sums is AND of OR terms (maxterms or larger sums). Both can represent any Boolean function. Canonical SOP lists every true minterm; canonical POS lists every false maxterm.

guide: Enter a function and read SOP and POS.
Compare canonical (one term per row) with a reduced form.
Toggle inputs and see which SOP term is active.
Switch to the terms tab if you need minterm numbers.
takeaways: SOP is a union of the 1-rows.
POS is a union of constraints from the 0-rows.
Canonical forms are unique; reduced forms are not.
forms.what: SOP and POS are two writings of the same output column.
forms.why: Gate networks follow the form: AND-OR for SOP, OR-AND for POS.
forms.notice: Don't-cares are handled on the truth-table and K-map studios.

theory.title: Minterms and maxterms
theory.body: A minterm is a product that is 1 for exactly one assignment (m0, m1, …). A maxterm is a sum that is 0 for exactly one assignment (M0, M1, …). Canonical SOP is the OR of the true minterms. Canonical POS is the AND of the false maxterms.

guide: Enter an expression and list minterm indices.
Read the matching maxterms for the 0-rows.
Toggle variables and see which minterm number is live.
Write Y as Σm(…) or ΠM(…).
takeaways: Minterm index is the binary value of the assignment.
Each 1-row contributes one minterm to canonical SOP.
Each 0-row contributes one maxterm to canonical POS.
terms.what: The index is the row number in the truth table.
terms.why: Numbering minterms lets you talk about a function without drawing every gate.
terms.notice: Variable order A, B, C with A as MSB matches the table in this lab.

theory.title: Karnaugh maps
theory.body: A K-map lays minterms in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ by one variable. A group of 1, 2, 4, or 8 (power of two), including wraparound, drops the variables that change inside the group. Don't-cares may join a group but need not be covered.

guide: Choose 2 to 6 variables.
Cycle cells through 0, 1, and X.
Read each group's product term.
Include a wraparound pair if the 1s sit on opposite edges.
takeaways: Adjacent cells differ by one variable.
Group size must be a power of two.
Don't-cares may be used but need not be covered.
map.what: Cell order is Gray code, so neighbors differ by one bit.
map.why: A power-of-two group eliminates the variables that change inside it.
map.notice: A dashed group wraps around the map edge.

theory.title: Prime implicants
theory.body: A prime implicant is a largest legal group that is not contained in a larger one. An essential prime is the only prime that covers some minterm — it must appear in every minimal cover. The remaining primes are chosen to cover leftovers at least cost.

guide: Fill 1s, then open this tab.
Read which primes are essential.
See leftover minterms that still need a prime.
Compare the selected cover with the map groups.
takeaways: Essential primes are the only cover for some minterm.
A prime is maximal: growing it would include a 0.
Cost here is how many gates the cover implies.
primes.what: The engine lists primes from the same map you edited.
primes.why: Picking non-essential primes is how two students get two equally short SOPs.
primes.notice: This is the covering step, not a different Boolean algebra.

theory.title: Quine–McCluskey
theory.body: Quine–McCluskey is tabular minimization: combine minterms that differ by one bit, repeat, then cover the 1s with primes. It does the same job as a K-map without drawing cells, so it scales past six variables in textbooks (this lab stays small and visible).

guide: Read the combination table from the current 1s and X's.
Follow which pairs merge by one bit.
See the prime chart and the chosen cover.
Compare the expression with the map tab.
takeaways: Merging two terms that differ by one bit drops that variable.
The prime chart is a covering problem.
QM and the K-map agree on this function.
qm.what: Each merge is a larger implicant.
qm.why: The algorithm is mechanical so it does not rely on seeing adjacency.
qm.notice: Don't-cares may be used in merges and need not be covered at the end.

theory.title: Before and after grouping
theory.body: Canonical SOP is one AND per minterm, then an OR. After grouping, fewer, wider ANDs feed a smaller OR. Gate count and depth drop when implicants cover several 1s. The two circuits must match on every input.

guide: Compare gate count before and after.
Toggle inputs and confirm both circuits agree.
Return to the map if a group looks wrong.
Note that don't-cares can shrink the after circuit.
takeaways: Fewer terms usually means fewer gates.
Depth follows the longest AND-OR path.
Equivalence is the truth table, not the drawing.
circuit.what: Both networks implement the same output column.
circuit.why: Simplification is worth it only if the function is unchanged.
circuit.notice: Counts are teaching gates, not a synthesizer report.

guide: Pick a size, then toggle address bits or click a cell.
Read needs CE and OE high. Write needs CE and WE high.
Watch the selected word in binary, hex, and decimal.
Turn CE off and try again — the array stays idle.
takeaways: Capacity = words × bits per word. Address lines = n for 2ⁿ locations.
CE gates the chip. OE drives the bus. WE updates the cell.
Only one word is selected at a time.
array.what: An address names one word in the array. Control pins decide whether that word is driven or stored.
array.why: Without CE/OE/WE the same cells would fight the bus or change on every address tick.
array.notice: A 16-cell window is drawn so a larger map stays readable.

guide: Write 0x5A into RAM — the cell updates.
Select ROM and write again — the word is rejected.
Program PROM twice to see the second write refused.
Program EPROM, then UV-erase the chip and program it again.
takeaways: RAM is read/write. Mask ROM is factory data.
PROM is one-shot. EPROM erases with UV (whole chip).
EEPROM erases a byte. Flash erases a block.
types.what: Volatility and erase grain decide whether a write sticks.
types.why: Firmware, look-up tables, and working storage are different jobs.
types.notice: These are teaching models of the write/erase rules, not silicon timing.

guide: Flip the SRAM bit — it stays until you flip it again.
Select a DRAM cell, press Decay, then Refresh.
When charge is low, a teaching read is marked unreliable.
Compare 6T feedback with a 1T capacitor.
takeaways: SRAM stores a bit in a cross-coupled loop. No refresh.
DRAM stores charge on a capacitor. Leakage forces refresh.
The bars are an abstraction, not a SPICE model.
cells.what: The same addressable array can be built from SRAM or DRAM cells.
cells.why: Density versus speed: DRAM packs more bits; SRAM holds them without a refresh timer.
cells.notice: This lab has its own DRAM array so it does not overwrite the RAM array tab.

guide: Change words and width — capacity and address pins update.
Click a cell in the matrix: row bits are RAS, column bits are CAS.
Toggle CE, OE, and WE on the chip drawing.
Match pin counts to the formula 2ⁿ × m.
takeaways: An n × m chip has n address pins and m data pins.
Large arrays are 2-D: row then column.
CE/OE/WE are the three control pins on a typical RAM.
org.what: Organization is how words and bits are arranged on the pins.
org.why: The CPU sees a linear address; the chip internally uses a row and a column.
org.notice: The matrix shows at most 8×8 of the array so the grid stays interactive.

guide: Toggle the n-bit select. Exactly one word line Yk goes high.
Turn Enable off — every output drops to 0.
Flip CPU address bits. Orange bits pick the chip; blue bits are the offset.
Watch the 3-to-8 chip decoder and the 8K map light the same chip.
takeaways: An n-to-2ⁿ decoder is one-hot: one Y line per address.
High-order bits are chip select. Low-order bits are the offset inside the chip.
Enable (often CE) blanks every output when the chip is idle.
decode.what: The decoder turns a binary address into one word line, and high bits into one chip-select.
decode.why: A CPU address bus is shared. Only the matching chip and matching word may respond.
decode.notice: 16-bit CPU space with 8K×8 chips needs 3 select bits and 13 offset bits.

guide: Raise the number of nibble chips — the data bus gets wider.
Raise the number of address chips — the space gets deeper.
Move the probe address and see which chip’s CS is high.
Compare shared address (word) with extra CS bits (address).
takeaways: Word expansion concatenates data pins. Address is shared.
Address expansion uses extra high bits as chip selects.
Both are how you build 64K from 8K parts.
expand.what: Systems are built from several smaller chips, not one giant die.
expand.why: Available parts have a fixed width and depth. Wiring them together makes the CPU’s memory map.
expand.notice: Each teaching chip is 1K words. Counts of 2 or 4 keep the map countable by hand.

guide: Step a burst of consecutive addresses in low-order mode.
Switch to high-order and step again — they stay in one bank.
Read bank, offset, and the address bits that chose the bank.
Think about why a cache line prefers low-order interleaving.
takeaways: Low-order interleaving spreads sequential addresses across banks.
High-order keeps a contiguous region in one bank.
Independent banks can start overlapping accesses.
banks.what: Interleaving is how consecutive addresses are assigned to parallel memories.
banks.why: A burst wants every next word in a different bank so requests can overlap.
banks.notice: This 16-word map makes the two policies visible without a DRAM datasheet.

guide: Choose Read or Write and step the cursor along the waveform.
Match Address → CE → OE/WE → data.
On the live chip, drop OE and try a read — the bus stays off.
Drop WE and try a write — the cell does not change.
takeaways: Address must be valid before CE.
Read uses OE. Write uses WE. They are not the same pin.
Setup and hold are why the waveform is ordered.
timing.what: A memory cycle is a sequence of control edges, not a single assignment.
timing.why: The array needs time to decode, drive, or store. The waveform is that contract.
timing.notice: Step times are educational units, not nanoseconds from a datasheet.

guide: Type a value in decimal (or choose another base).
See the equivalent value in binary, octal, and hexadecimal update instantly.
Understand how each digit contributes to the total value.
Experiment with larger or smaller values and notice the patterns.
takeaways: The value of a digit depends on its position (place value).
Binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal are different ways to represent the same number.
Grouping 3 bits (octal) or 4 bits (hexadecimal) makes conversion simple and consistent.
convert.what: All representations update automatically when you change the input number.
convert.why: Each base uses a different positional value, but they represent the same quantity.
convert.notice: Grouping binary digits into 3 or 4 bits makes conversion to octal or hexadecimal straightforward.

guide: Type values for A and B. Change the word size if needed.
Try addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division.
See each column’s calculation, including carries or borrows.
Experiment with larger numbers and watch how the steps change.
takeaways: Binary addition uses carries when the sum is 2 or more.
Binary subtraction uses borrows when needed.
Binary multiplication uses shifted partial products.
Binary division finds the quotient using repeated subtraction or long division.
The same column-by-column rules apply as in decimal, just with base 2.
math.what: All representations update automatically when you change the inputs or operation.
math.why: Binary arithmetic is the foundation for how computers perform calculations in hardware.
math.notice: Carries move left in addition, borrows move left in subtraction, and multiplication uses shifted partial products.

guide: Type a decimal number (positive or negative) and choose a word size (4, 8, or 16 bits).
See the sign-magnitude, one’s complement, and two’s complement forms update instantly.
Notice how negative numbers are encoded differently in each method.
Use the range visualization to understand the minimum and maximum values for the selected word size.
takeaways: The MSB indicates the sign (0 = positive, 1 = negative).
Sign-magnitude and one’s complement have two zeros (+0 and −0).
Two’s complement is the most common method and makes arithmetic straightforward.
signed.what: All representations update automatically when you change the input number or word size.
signed.why: Different signed representations exist, but they represent the same numeric value.
signed.notice: Sign-magnitude and one’s complement have two zeros (+0 and −0), while two’s complement has a single zero.

guide: Choose integer bits and fractional bits (Q format).
Type a decimal value (positive or negative) and see the encoded binary representation.
See how each bit contributes to the value using fixed place values around the binary point.
Change the number of fractional bits to see the effect on step size, range, and precision.
takeaways: A fixed binary point means values are multiples of a fixed step size (2⁻ᶠʳᵃᶜᵗⁱᵒⁿᵃˡ ᵇⁱᵗˢ).
More fractional bits give finer resolution but a smaller integer range for a fixed total width.
Fixed-point is widely used in embedded systems, DSP, and hardware where floating point is unnecessary.
fixed.what: All representations update automatically when you change the format or input value.
fixed.why: The fractional bits fix the binary point position, so values represent multiples of a fixed step size.
fixed.notice: More fractional bits give finer resolution (smaller steps). With a fixed total width, they reduce the integer range.

guide: Type a floating-point number (e.g., 13.625) and choose single or double precision.
See how the value is split into sign, exponent, and fraction bits, and view the hexadecimal form.
Learn about the exponent bias (127 for single, 1023 for double) and how it determines the actual exponent.
Enter 0, a very small number, infinity, or NaN to see their bit patterns.
takeaways: IEEE-754 uses 1 sign bit, a biased exponent, and a fraction (mantissa).
The exponent bias is 127 (single) or 1023 (double).
Normalized numbers have an implicit leading 1 in the fraction.
Special bit patterns represent zero, subnormal numbers, infinity, and NaN.
ieee.what: When you change the decimal value or precision, all fields update automatically — sign, exponent, fraction, and hexadecimal.
ieee.why: IEEE-754 uses a biased exponent and an implicit leading 1 for normalized numbers, which increases range and precision.
ieee.notice: The same real number has different bit patterns in single and double precision due to different exponent and fraction sizes.

guide: Type a decimal number (e.g., 59) or a character (e.g., A).
See how the value is encoded in BCD, Gray code, Excess-3, and ASCII instantly.
Look at multiple examples to understand the differences between codes.
Experiment with other numbers and characters to see patterns and when each code is useful.
takeaways: BCD encodes each decimal digit using 4 bits and is common in displays and calculators.
Gray code changes only one bit between adjacent values, reducing errors in position sensing.
Excess-3 is BCD with 3 added to each digit.
ASCII encodes characters, numbers, and symbols for text representation in computers.
codes.what: All representations update automatically when you change the input value or code type.
codes.why: Different codes are optimized for different uses such as displays, position sensing, error reduction, or representing text.
codes.notice: Gray code changes only one bit between adjacent values, while Excess-3 and BCD are designed for decimal digits, and ASCII encodes text.

guide: Enter a bit string, choose even or odd parity, and see the resulting code word and checksum.
Flip bits in the received stream and see whether the error is detected.
See how polynomial division produces a small remainder used as a CRC.
Experiment with different data and generators to build intuition.
takeaways: Parity adds one bit and detects all single-bit errors (but misses some multi-bit errors).
Checksums add a small value computed from the data and can detect many common errors.
CRC uses polynomial division to produce a remainder that detects a wide range of error patterns.
parity.what: This page focuses on error detection using parity, checksums, and CRC, with an interactive simulator and visual explanations.
parity.why: Redundancy lets the receiver detect when bits have been altered during transmission or storage, increasing reliability.
parity.notice: Error detection tells us that an error occurred, but it usually does not tell us which bit is wrong or fix it — that is the job of error correction codes.

guide: Type a 4-bit data word (e.g., 1011). See parity bits placed at positions 1, 2, and 4.
Flip a bit in the received word to simulate a single-bit error. Watch the parity checks and syndrome.
Read the syndrome (s2 s1 s0) and see the decimal position of the error.
The bit at the indicated position is flipped to recover the original data word.
takeaways: Parity bits are placed at positions 1, 2, 4, … (powers of 2).
Each parity bit checks a specific set of positions based on the binary index.
A non-zero syndrome gives the 1-based position of a single-bit error.
Hamming code (7,4) corrects any single-bit error (SEC).
hamming.what: As you enter the data word or flip a received bit, parity bits, syndrome, and correction update automatically.
hamming.why: Each parity bit checks a different set of positions (1, 2, 4, …). The syndrome bits identify the index of a single-bit error in binary.
hamming.notice: A zero syndrome means no error is detected. A non-zero syndrome gives the 1-based position to flip, correcting a single-bit error.

theory.title: Clock frequency and duty
theory.body: Period is 1 / frequency. Duty cycle is high time over period. This waveform is simulated time so you can mark edges; it is not a lab oscillator.

guide: Set frequency and read the period.
Change duty and see the high pulse width.
Move the cursor along the samples.
Open Edges to name rise versus fall.
takeaways: Period is the reciprocal of frequency.
Duty cycle is high time over period.
Simulated nanoseconds, not a wall-clock wait.

theory.title: Clock edges
theory.body: A rising edge is 0→1. A falling edge is 1→0. Flip-flops in this curriculum sample on an edge you choose. The event is the transition, not the level that follows.

guide: Mark a rising edge on the waveform.
Compare rise and fall lists.
Move phase and see edges slide.
Remember: capture happens at the edge, not during the high pulse.
takeaways: Rise is 0→1; fall is 1→0.
Edge-triggered storage ignores the level between edges.
Phase slides the whole pattern.

theory.title: Setup time
theory.body: Setup is how long D must be stable before the capturing edge. If D arrives too late, the sampled value is uncertain (X in this lab). Setup is a before-the-edge window.

guide: Place D so it settles before the edge.
Move D later until the capture is X.
Read the setup window on the waveform.
Compare with the hold tab: that window is after the edge.
takeaways: Setup is before the capturing edge.
A late D makes the capture uncertain.
X here means uncertain, not a transistor waveform.

theory.title: Hold time
theory.body: Hold is how long D must remain stable after the capturing edge. Changing D too soon can corrupt the new state. Hold is an after-the-edge window.

guide: Keep D stable past the edge.
Pull D back too early and read X.
Contrast with setup on the previous tab.
Think of hold as 'don't let go yet'.
takeaways: Hold is after the capturing edge.
An early D change makes the capture uncertain.
Setup and hold together are the aperture around the edge.

theory.title: Propagation through combinational logic
theory.body: The next flip-flop must not sample until the combinational path from the previous edge has settled. That path delay plus setup must fit in one period.

guide: Change the delay and watch when Y becomes valid.
See the next edge arrive before Y settles — a teaching setup fail.
Relate period ≥ delay + setup.
This is the same delay idea as the gate studio, now next to a clock.
takeaways: Period must cover logic delay plus setup.
A too-fast clock samples stale or uncertain data.
Delay here is a teaching number, not a cell library.

theory.title: Metastability
theory.body: If D is changing inside the aperture, the flip-flop can sit between 0 and 1 for a while. This lab shows that as X and a note — it is not a SPICE tail. Synchronizers are extra stages to make that rare.

guide: Aim D at the edge and read the metastable note.
Move D clearly before or after to get a clean 0 or 1.
Treat X as 'do not trust this sample'.
Two stages (a synchronizer) are the usual teaching fix.
takeaways: Sampling a moving D can be metastable.
X means the value is not a legal 0 or 1 yet.
This is a concept demo, not a MTBF calculator.
